author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: A festal homily celebrating the day of the Annunciation, when Gabriel came to the Virgin Mary and announced the conception of Jesus Christ.
argument: The homily opens by proclaiming that the mystery hidden from eternity is now made known, and that God crowns the faithful on this feast day. It declares the fulfillment of David's oracle that the heavens and earth rejoice at the Lord's coming, and connects this joy to Christ's promise of lasting joy to believers. The central narrative recounts Gabriel's greeting to Mary, her question, and the angel's answer that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the child will be called Son of God. The text breaks off with an incomplete sentence fragment about Mary alone among all generations, leaving the conclusion unfinished.

outline.move: The homily announces the revelation of the hidden mystery, the crowning of the faithful, the fulfillment of David's prophecy, and recounts the Annunciation dialogue between Gabriel and Mary, ending with an incomplete sentence about Mary.

voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'Dixit autem Maria ad Angelum' and quoted directly.

key_terms.sense: The divine secret hidden from eternity, now revealed in the Annunciation.
Crowns woven for the faithful on this feast day, signifying reward and honor.
The status of the faithful as called and heirs of the heavenly kingdom.
The lasting joy announced to Christians who hope in Christ.
The angel's greeting to Mary, indicating she has found favor with God.
The Holy Spirit, who will come upon Mary and cause the conception.
The power of the Most High that will overshadow Mary.
The title of the child to be born, indicating his divine nature.
The title given to Jesus, indicating his divine sonship.
The heavenly choirs of bodiless beings whose ministry the faithful are called to join.

scripture: The author quotes the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering and cites David as the speaker. The quotation 'Laetentur caeli, et exultet terra...' corresponds to Psalm 95:11-13 in the Septuagint (Psalm 96:11-13 in the Hebrew/Masoretic numbering). The Annunciation dialogue follows Luke 1:28-35. Modern citations should use the Hebrew Psalm numbering with a note where the LXX differs.
uncertain: The precise date of composition is unknown.
The original language of the homily is uncertain; the surviving text is Latin, but it may be a translation from Greek.
The addressee or original audience is not specified in the text.
The text ends with an incomplete sentence fragment, so the intended conclusion is unknown.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text breaks off with an incomplete sentence fragment about Mary alone among all generations, leaving the conclusion unfinished.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Convenienter igitur sanctam Mariam ex omnibus generationibus solam.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text ends with an incomplete sentence: 'Convenienter igitur sanctam Mariam ex omnibus generationibus solam.' ('Therefore fittingly [he chose/appointed] holy Mary alone from all generations...'). The participle or finite verb is missing, but the sentence is clearly incomplete rather than a mere 'fragment'—it has a grammatical subject and modifier but lacks a main verb.

_unresolved_facts.claim: John the Baptist is not explicitly named
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Forerunner is identified only as 'Praecursor vero Domini' ('the Forerunner of the Lord'). The identification with John the Baptist is traditional but not explicit in the text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: 'Ave gratia plena' is reported speech introduced by 'adnuntiat'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: illud Ave gratia plena ipsi adnuntiat
_unresolved_facts.fix: 'Ave gratia plena' is presented as a quotation in indirect discourse ('illud Ave gratia plena ipsi adnuntiat'—'he announces to her that 'Hail, full of grace''), not as reported speech. The direct quotation begins with 'Dominus tecum' introduced by 'dicens'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The author quotes the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering and cites David as the speaker.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Davidicum adimpletum est oraculum, quod dicit: Laetentur caeli, et exultet terra. Gaudebunt campi, et omnia ligna silvae a conspectu Domini, quoniam venit.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text attributes the oracle to David ('Davidicum... oraculum, quod dicit'), but the quotation 'Laetentur caeli...' corresponds to Psalm 96:11-13 (Hebrew/Masoretic) / Psalm 95:11-13 (LXX). The brief's claim about 'Septuagint numbering' is anachronistic for the author's own practice—medieval and patristic writers typically used the Septuagint numbering, but the brief should simply note that the text follows the LXX tradition in attributing this to David.
